title: Schema in Plain Words: Three Types Most Businesses Need
h1: Schema in plain words: three types most businesses need
desc: Schema is a label system that describes your page to machines. Learn the three types most small businesses use and the one rule that keeps them safe.
lead: Schema is a way of labelling your page so a machine knows what each part is: a business, a product, a question. Most small businesses need only three types, and one rule.
body:
"Schema" sounds technical, but the idea is simple. It is a set of labels, agreed across the web, that you add to a page so machines know exactly what they are reading: this is a business, this is its phone number, this is a product with this price. The labels sit in the page code, in a format called JSON-LD. A developer or a plugin usually adds them.

First, an honest note: Google says no special markup is required for its AI features. Structured data is a documented way to describe a page. It is not a switch that guarantees visibility. See the schema glossary entry.

The one rule

Everything in the schema must match what a visitor can see on the page. Never label something that is not there.

Mismatches, such as a price in the code that differs from the price on the page, create confusion and can cause problems. Keep them identical.

The three types

  1. Organization or LocalBusiness. Describes who you are: name, logo, website, contact details, and for a local business the address and opening hours. Put it on your homepage or About page. Use LocalBusiness if customers visit you.
  2. Product (or Service). Describes what you sell: name, description, price, currency and availability. Put it on each product page, and keep it in sync with the visible price.
  3. FAQPage. Describes questions and answers that appear on the page. Only use it if the questions and answers are visible to the visitor, word for word.

What goes where

TypePageMatches what the visitor sees
Organization / LocalBusinessHome, AboutName, address, phone, hours
ProductEach product pageName, price, availability
FAQPagePages with a real FAQThe visible questions and answers

A small example

This is a minimal Organization block. The values are placeholders, so replace every one with your real details.

<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Organization",
  "name": "Example Co",
  "url": "https://example.com",
  "logo": "https://example.com/logo.png"
}
</script>

How to check it

  • Ask your developer or plugin where the schema is added, and on which pages.
  • Use a structured data testing tool, such as Google's Rich Results Test, to check there are no errors.
  • Compare each value in the schema with the visible page.
  • Update the schema whenever you change prices, hours or contact details.

From my work

At Qoyod I used Schema on template pages together with answer-first rewrites of page openings and internal links between new content. I can't isolate schema's own contribution from the rest, and I don't claim to.

What to do next

If you only have time for one thing, add an accurate Organization or LocalBusiness block to your homepage. Then test whether tools describe you correctly with the free visibility test. For the technical checks, use the technical checklist with your developer.
faq: Do I need schema to appear in AI answers?
Google says no special markup is required for its AI features. Schema is a documented way to describe a page accurately.
Only if it does not match the visible page. Keep every value identical to what visitors see.
Who adds schema to my site?
Usually a developer or an SEO plugin. Give them the three types and the matching rule.
